Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

Memory.value: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: People are not what they seem

vignette: Evelyn, a 37‑year‑old violinist from Detroit, remembers the night of the bombing as if the concert hall had never been a safe place. The city’s grand theater was packed with families and friends for the premiere of a new concerto. She was onstage, bow poised, her heart racing with anticipation. Suddenly, a deafening explosion tore through the foyer. Light flashed, a plume of smoke filled the air, and the sound of shattered glass drowned out the music. In that instant she felt herself fall from the stage, her breath caught, and the world turned into a storm of noise and fear. When the police arrived, the chaos was still palpable; the scent of burning plastic clung to the air like a second skin. Evelyn’s voice onstage was replaced by the roar of her own pulse. The event left a scar that would follow her wherever she played. The first time Evelyn realized how the memory haunted her was during a rehearsal a week later. She was trying to master a difficult passage, but every time she placed her fingers on the correct string, a flash of the explosion’s light rushed into her mind. Her mind would then cut back to the stage, her breathing shallow, the taste of burnt plastic and coffee that had been in her hand during the blast. “When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once,” she told me, her voice trembling. The threat of being surrounded by a crowded hall—loud applause, the murmur of a crowd, even the simple sound of a microphone—was enough to bring her back to the front row, feeling the ground shift beneath her. This threat‑driven flashback disrupted her concentration, leaving her unable to focus on the notes she had practiced for weeks. The irritability that followed her onstage during that evening was not merely frustration; it was a protective reaction to the sudden feeling that the world had shifted to a place where danger lurked behind every curtain. The vivid, sensory‑rich memories of the terror, however, did more than just cause flashbacks. The clarity and detail of the images—“My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed” – amplified the sense that the event was not merely a past occurrence, but a persistent threat. The taste she could summon each time she recalled the explosion made the memory feel as fresh as that night. Evelyn’s thoughts swirled, “I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns,” and the taste was a reminder that the danger was not over. This relentless recollection fed her negative appraisals. She came to believe that she no longer belonged anywhere, that people are not what they seem, and that she has no future. Each recollection reinforced the idea that she was unsafe and that the world had turned against her. Conversely, her negative appraisals fueled the intensity of the memories. As Evelyn began to see her colleagues as unreliable, as audiences as potentially hostile, the context in which she imagined the concert hall changed. The very act of believing that people are not what they seem cast the memory of the bombing into a darker light. The fear that she would be judged or betrayed made the memory more urgent, making the taste of burnt plastic feel even more urgent and real. In this way, the negative appraisal loop tightened the grasp of the traumatic memory, and the memory further entrenched those negative beliefs. For months, the cycle of threat, memory, and negative appraisal continued to erode Evelyn’s ability to perform. The same sounds that once exhilarated her now triggered the flashback, and her frustration led to angry outbursts that left her colleagues wary. Her relationship with her partner suffered because the partner’s supportive words were often dismissed as “not what they seem,” a product of her distrust. Evelyn’s concentration suffered so badly that she missed a rehearsal entirely and almost lost her next performance slot. She finally sought help after a rehearsal in which, in the middle of a passage, she felt herself freeze and taste the metallic tang of fear so strongly that she could not finish the bow. She realized that her life as a musician, the place where she felt she belonged, had become a battlefield. Evelyn came to the clinic clutching her score, her fingers trembling on the strings. She was most afraid that the memories would continue to strip her of her career and her sense of place, and she hoped to regain control over her concentration and her relationships. The next session, she described her fear that she would no longer belong anywhere, and she asked for help to break the cycle that had turned the memory of a single night into an all‑encompassing threat.
